How a mild 10 per cent tax became 25 per cent

footnote.text: The taxman giveth and the taxman taketh away.

brief.head: Empire on a tenth
brief.text: The UK of 1910 ruled the world on about 10 per cent of GDP, Ajay Shah said. The size of the Indian state, in his view, is way overdone. {121-C03}

brief.head: Square the rate
brief.text: Economic distortion rises roughly with the square of the tax rate, Shah said. Going from 8 or 9 per cent to 16 or 18 multiplies it by four. {#fourx}

brief.head: Late is a tax too
brief.text: When input tax credit comes back slowly, firms pay interest on working capital the government holds. That interest, Shah said, is itself a tax. {#late}

brief.head: Give me tariffs
brief.text: Cascading taxes make a foreign shirt at 300 look cheap beside an Indian one at 440, Shah said, and domestic firms then lobby for tariffs. {#tariffs}

brief.head: Ideas come first
brief.text: Busy civil servants are mostly firefighting, Shah said. Real progress in India happens upstream of policymakers: in papers, books, blogs and seminars. {121-C10}

thought.text: Tax policy doesn’t exist to serve the state.

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on the tax he helped name, and how to mend it
lead.head: The tax that lost its heart
body: A few mornings earlier, the *Business Standard* had carried a column by Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah on how India’s GST could be made much better. Policymakers, Amit Varma said, “squealed in delight, unless they were part of government, where they squealed in embarrassment”.
The same three had written the paper that first brought the GST into Indian policy circles. They did not like the shape it took, Varma said.

Shah’s diagnosis was stark. The GST was meant to be a value added tax, and a VAT lives by the flow of input tax credit from one stage of production to the next. In India, that flow is increasingly blocked.
“If you don’t have correct handling of input tax credit, then it’s not a VAT,” he said. “Then you’re back to production tax, you’re back to cascading taxes.” {121-C08}
## Growth first

Shah began where, he said, every question about the state should begin: economic growth. Growth comes from high-productivity firms, and they rest on three pillars: specialisation, learning by doing and globalisation.
“So the job of the tax system is never ever mess with these three,” he said. “Do not come in the way.” {121-C01}
A cascading tax, charged on every sale, does exactly that. It taxes tax on tax, and in Shah’s worked example a “mild” 10 per cent on each sale of a 400-rupee shirt ended up as 25 per cent.
Among economists, he said, “bad tax” is no mild phrase: “bad taxes are mind-blowingly stupid things that only an idiot would ever do.” {121-C04}
Such taxes punish specialisation and hobble exporters.
## Taxing the value added
The way out, Shah said, was one of the great advances of 20th-century economics: the value added tax, invented by the French economist Maurice Lauré in 1954.
Each seller deducts the tax already paid upstream. Run the same shirt through a VAT and the government collects 40 rupees, a true 10 per cent, however the work is split among firms.
“The travel of input tax credit is the engine, is the heart of the VAT,” Shah said. {121-C05}
Exports are zero-rated, so goods compete abroad at tax-free prices. And a good VAT has a low rate, a single rate and a comprehensive base.
## A tax in name
India’s GST, announced in 2016 and launched in 2017, broke all three of those rules: many rates, cesses, and whole sectors such as electricity, petroleum and real estate left out.
Worse, Shah said, the blockages keep spreading. Some goods taxed at 5 per cent have their credit blocked, so the real burden is far higher.
Varma, who had long called the GST great in concept and terrible in implementation, said he had not known how many ways the credit was being blocked.
The hosts traced the drift to who writes tax policy. Power has shifted to the tax administrators of the Department of Revenue, and in the meetings that block credit, nobody asks about GDP.

The fix, Shah said, is the original prescription, beginning with the removal of every blockage. “So the answer is exactly where we were in 2003,” he said. “Have a single rate, have a low rate, with a comprehensive base, and I’m embarrassed to say with no blockages against input tax credit.” {121-C11}
“It is a long game, it is a hard fight,” Varma said.
lead.reelLabel: Hear the case for a fix

second.label: Origin story
second.head: A VAT by any other name
second.deck: Why Ajay Shah and his co-authors coined ‘goods and services tax’ in 2003
body: In 2003, Vijay Kelkar led a committee, appointed by Jaswant Singh, on implementing the FRBM Act. Working on it, Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah concluded that India’s fiscal problem had no way out without a proper VAT. {121-S02}
There was a snag. The word was taken. A central VAT, CENVAT, was starting to happen, but it was not a VAT: it did not handle input tax credit or services correctly.
So they coined a new name, Shah said, to avoid explaining “the twenty ways in which that was not quite a VAT”. The name appeared in a committee report in 2003. {#report}

quote.text: So we coined the phrase goods and services tax as a way to just distinguish to make sure there’s no confusion

second.caption: why it is not called VAT

third.head: Tax-free on the high seas
body: When an Indian shirt is sold to a foreigner, Ajay Shah said, a good VAT charges no tax at all. The exporter also claims back the input tax credit built up along the way. {121-C06}
“You do not tax foreigners. Don’t bring nationalism into this,” he said, brushing aside talk of a level playing field. Good taxation, he said, is not populistic.
On the high seas, then, the shirt’s price is immune to taxation, and countries with high and low VAT rates compete on equal terms.

At its destination the shirt pays the local VAT. “The French are very socialist,” Shah said, “so they have a 20% VAT.” {121-J08} The importer pays 80 rupees at the border, and a French shirtmaker faces the same 20 per cent.
third.caption: zero-rating of exports

p2.title: How to fix our GST
p2.deck: From growth to the fix: Ajay Shah, one of the authors of the original GST paper, on what went wrong

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Just grow your own Google
sections.caption: the three engines of firm productivity
body: Every question about the state, Ajay Shah said, should start with economic growth. And growth is easy: “You just have to get NVIDIA and Google emerge out of the Indian soil.” {121-J02}
High-productivity firms, he said, have three ingredients. The first is specialisation, Adam Smith’s pin idea: a jack of all trades is a master of none.

The second is learning by doing, via Wright’s Law and cost experience curves. Shah borrowed Amit Varma’s phrase for it: put in volume. “If you’ve made 10,000 pins, you ain’t seen nothing yet.” {121-J11}
The third is globalisation: removing the thicket of barriers at the border to capital, labour, goods, services and enterprise.
Varma pointed to the show’s episode on Lant Pritchett’s work: every human welfare indicator depends on per capita GDP rising, and growth is the only way out of poverty.
## A small state
The state, Shah said, needs money for peace, easy taxes, a tolerable administration of justice and a few basics. He would rather the Indian state taxed less and spent less. {121-C03}

Offer a policymaker 15 rupees of tax on a GDP of 100, or 15 on a GDP of 200, and too many in Indian taxation see no difference. Shah would take the bigger GDP: tax policy exists to serve the people. {121-C02}
~ The tax system’s one duty, Shah said, is to stay out of the way of the three engines of firm productivity.

quote.text: In about 10% of GDP, you can become the UK of 1910.

sections.label: The bad tax
sections.head: The monster in the invoice
sections.caption: the cascading tax on production
body: Among economists, Ajay Shah said, “bad tax” is not a mild phrase. A handful of taxes are good, and every other scheme known to man is bad.
One example is the cascading tax, levied at every stage of production. A 10 per cent tax on each sale of a shirt, from cotton to customer, adds up to 25 per cent. {121-S01}

It strikes at two of the three pillars of growth. Firms stop specialising, because one company that runs from petrochemicals to cloth escapes the tax on each sale. “And I have a suggested brand name for that cloth,” Shah said. “It’s called Vimal.” {121-J04}
## Bad for trade

Exporters suffer too. How, Shah asked, can an Indian shirtmaker compete with “a country with brilliant Bengali economists who have constructed a superior tax system? It’s called Bangladesh.” {121-J06}
And imports look cheap, so domestic firms ask for tariffs: “another nightmare”.
Shah thought every God-fearing economist should stand up and stage a dharna. Amit Varma demurred: “Our economists don’t fear God. They fear government.” {121-J05}
~ Varma, for his part, felt like starting a hashtag: not all taxes. {121-J03}

quote.text: It sounds like a nice meek five percent tax, but it’s actually something truly terrible.

sections.label: The French answer
sections.head: Credit where it’s due
sections.caption: the value added tax and input tax credit
body: One of the great advances of 20th-century economics, Ajay Shah said, was the value added tax, invented by the French economist Maurice Lauré in 1954. Anyone who thinks economics is “the boring game of sitting in an office and writing R programs” should think again. {121-J10}
The idea is to tax not production but the value added at each stage. Every seller charges tax on its invoice, but deducts the tax already paid upstream, which reaches it as input tax credit.

Run the 400-rupee shirt through this and each stage remits just 10 rupees: 40 in all, a true 10 per cent. One firm or four, the tax is the same. “The government has no view,” Shah said, on how specialised firms should be.
## The export trick
Exports are zero-rated. The exporter charges no VAT and claims a refund of all its accumulated credit, so exporters everywhere compete on tax-free prices. {121-C06}
Without the travel of credit, Shah warned, it is not a VAT at all, just a production tax “with all those deleterious outcomes”. {121-C05}
~ Amit Varma called it “such a beautiful, elegant design”.

quote.text: this simple idea is transformative because it becomes neutral to the complexity of the production process.

sections.label: Getting it right
sections.head: Paratha at 18, roti at 5
sections.caption: a low, single rate on a broad base
body: A VAT done right, Ajay Shah said, rests on three principles. The first is a low rate. “Don’t have a value added tax of 28 per cent. That is just nuts.” {#nuts}

His preferred rate for India is 8 per cent, at most 9. High rates push people to evade and back into cash. Distortion, he said, rises roughly with the square of the tax rate, so doubling the rate quadruples the damage. {121-C07}
The second is a comprehensive base with no exemptions. Shrink the base, and “the ever thirsty government” wants a higher rate. The path to a low rate lies in a broad base.
## Classification wars
The third is a single rate. Many rates, Shah said, invite jockeying, lobbying and corruption, and classification disputes: India has taxed parathas at 18 per cent and rotis at 5.
Amit Varma had the classic case: “is KitKat a chocolate or a biscuit?” {121-J12}
Multiple rates also strain a state of low capability, Shah said. Administering one low rate on everything is something India can manage.
~ His advice: “keep your life simple”.

quote.text: The distortion imposed upon an economy goes up roughly in proportion to the tax rate squared.

sections.label: The Indian journey
sections.head: From excise to a leaky GST
sections.caption: the blocking of input tax credit
body: India began with excise, a tax on production collected by an inspector at the factory gate, Ajay Shah said. {#excise} Later came a cascading tax on services.

In 2004 Chidambaram, as finance minister, chose not to pursue the GST, citing a lack of support in state governments. The BJP refused to take part in tax reform. Yet the authors had proposed a route around the states: the Centre could build the tax for itself and let states join later. {121-S03}
Arun Jaitley, as finance minister, revived it: the GST was announced in 2016 and launched in 2017. {#jaitley} It broke all three principles: many rates and cesses, whole sectors left out.
## Credit blocked

The gravest failure, Shah said, is the blocking of input tax credit. Final-stage goods producers do not get proper credit for services and capital goods, and services firms face blocks too. Several goods at 5 per cent have their credit blocked: “the taxman giveth and the taxman taketh away.” {121-J07}
Amit Varma recalled calling the GST “conceptually great, but the implementation was terrible”. His guest Devangshu Datta had predicted the failures before the tax was even announced. {121-S04}
~ The cure, Shah said, is to “run, not walk” and restore seamless end-to-end credit.

quote.text: So all the three principles of a good VAT were violated in the GST as it unfolded, as it came out the front door.

side.boxText: In a 2003 committee report, Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah coined the name GST. Now, in their column *To GST or not to GST*, they document how input tax credit has been blocked, and prescribe the same cure. {121-C11}

contQuote.text: The way we’ve always talked about it is that the most important change that happens in the country is upstream of policymakers. It is in the ideas, it is in the knowledge.

stories.caption: the 400-rupee shirt
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah follows one shirt from cotton to customer
stories.head: Ten per cent, four times over
body: A farmer sells cotton to a spinner for 100 rupees, Ajay Shah began. With a 10 per cent tax on every sale, 10 rupees go to the government.
The spinner sells yarn to a weaver for 200: another 20 rupees in tax. The fabric goes to a tailor for 300: 30 more. The tailor sells the shirt to a customer for 400: 40 more.
The customer pays 440 and may think 10 per cent is not so bad. But, as Amit Varma totted up, 100 rupees have gone to the government.
Once you see the whole chain, Shah said, you can’t unsee it. “On a 400 rupee shirt, the government got 100 rupees of tax,” he said. “That’s 25%.” {121-S01}
~ Then he ran the same shirt through a VAT. Each seller deducts the tax already paid upstream, so each stage sends only 10 rupees to the government. The total is 40: a true 10 per cent. {#forty}
stories.why: The same 10 per cent can mean 25 or 10 depending on design alone. What matters is not the headline rate but whether tax is piled on tax, which is why Shah counts the cascading tax among the bad taxes. {121-C04}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the road from a 2003 report to the GST
stories.head: A decade in the pending tray
body: Ajay Shah and his co-authors had proposed the GST in a 2003 committee report. They also offered a route that did not need every state on board: the Centre could build an integrated tax on goods and services for itself, and states could join later. {121-S03}
In 2004, Chidambaram, as finance minister, chose not to pursue it. Partly, Shah said, he cited a lack of support from state governments. The BJP said it would not take part in any tax policy reform.
“So the things were kicked forward till 2014,” Shah said. The Congress was in power for ten years. {#kicked}
Then Arun Jaitley, as finance minister, got back to the project. The GST was announced in 2016, launched in 2017 and has been amended many times since.
~ By then its rates were, in Shah’s words, “astronomically high”, and electricity, petroleum and real estate were left out.
stories.why: A good idea can be adopted in name and lose its core on the way. By the time the GST came out of the front door, Shah said, all three principles of a good VAT had been violated.
stories.postscript: Today, Shah said, the answer is exactly where it was in 2003. {121-C11}

stories.start: So you know when the scene and the unseen started in the early days
stories.end: And then later I had a comprehensive episode with Shruti Raj Gopalan as well.
stories.caption: demonetisation and the GST
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on demonetisation, the GST and an early warning
stories.head: Devangshu Datta saw it coming
body: In the early days of *The Seen and the Unseen*, Amit Varma said, episodes were not long deep dives. Each looked at one policy, and he did early episodes on demonetisation and many on the GST.

He judged the two very differently. “Demonetisation was just a disastrous policy measure, conceptually wrong, everything was bad about it,” he said. “But GST was conceptually great, but the implementation was terrible.” {121-S04}

His first GST guest was their friend Devangshu Datta, who correctly predicted everything that would go wrong, before the GST was even announced. A later episode with Shruti Rajagopalan was comprehensive.

~ Now, Varma said, Ajay Shah’s account of blocked input tax credit worried him deeply. Credit has to work properly, he said, or what is the point? He had not known it was blocked in so many ways. {#aware}
stories.why: Separate a policy’s concept from its execution. In Varma’s view, demonetisation was wrong on both counts and the GST only on the second, and an informed observer saw the failures coming.

quiz.a: The travel of input tax credit from one stage of production to the next.
